Why the age matters electrically

A building from 1906 was wired, if it was wired at all, for lighting. Everything since — the refrigerator, the window units, the home office, the induction range, the car — has been added to a service that was never designed for it. That is the single thread running through most Chicago electrical work.
Township by township

West Chicago is the oldest at 83% pre-1940 across 65,664 properties. Lake View follows at 71% across 23,046. Jefferson township — Portage Park, Jefferson Park, Irving Park — is younger at 60% pre-1940 but far larger at 112,923 properties, and its median year of 1927 puts most of it in the bungalow era. Rogers Park is the youngest of the north-side townships at a 1938 median.
What that means room by room

188,389 properties citywide are two-storey and 154,926 single-storey; 324,305 have full basements, which is where the panel usually lives and where access is usually straightforward. 107,336 properties have no garage at all — relevant the moment an EV charger enters the conversation. And 335,769 use a warm-air furnace against 98,849 on hot water or steam, which decides what kind of equipment circuits exist already.
Chicago publishes every permit it issues. That makes contractor claims checkable, including ours.

What we actually pull permits for

Our own job-type mix: 307 service or new service permits, 206 outlets and receptacles, 163 electrical panel, 162 200-amp service upgrades, 126 lighting, 117 100-amp service and 33 at 400 amp or larger. By permit route, 527 went through the Express Permit Program, 340 new construction and 325 renovation or alteration.
Where we work most
Ward 1 (129 permits), Ward 32 (85), Ward 26 (72), Ward 47 (68) and Ward 27 (63) lead our record — the north and northwest sides, consistent with a shop on N Lincoln Ave.
The citywide picture

Chicago issued 20,187 electrical permits in 24 months. Lighting leads at 9,748, outlets and receptacles at 9,306, service work at 6,672, panels at 5,219 and solar at 4,033. At the other end, rewires ran to 28 permits and ceiling fans to 3 — a useful corrective to any contractor telling you a whole-house rewire is routine.
One honest caveat

Permit values are the reported construction value of the whole project, which often includes trades other than ours. They are a good guide to the scale of a job and a poor guide to a contractor's revenue. We quote from scope, not from permit data.

faqs.question: Do I need a panel upgrade before solar?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. The array has to interconnect somewhere with capacity to spare. We assess the service first so the answer arrives before you sign, not during the install.

faqs.answer: Utility timelines vary and sit outside our control, which is exactly why we schedule around them rather than promising a date we cannot hold.

faqs.answer: Yes — ballasted or attached racking depending on the roof and the structure. Flat roofs are common here and are not an obstacle.

faqs.answer: If the roof has only a few years left, usually yes. Removing and reinstalling an array later adds cost. We check roof condition at the assessment and tell you if the roof should come first.

faqs.question: Will my solar panels work during a power outage?
faqs.answer: Not on their own. A grid-tied array shuts off in an outage, so it can't feed power into lines utility crews are working on. To keep power you need a battery, or a backup-capable inverter, set up to run the circuits you choose.

sections.heading: How panel capacity limits solar
sections.body: An array feeds power back through your panel. Electrical code caps how much it can feed, based on the panel's busbar rating and the size of its main breaker. A panel that is already full, or has a small busbar, may not have room even when it seems fine for everyday use. There are three ways around that: connect on the supply side of the main breaker, replace the panel with one that has a larger busbar, or upgrade the service. Which one fits depends on the panel, the meter arrangement and the building.

sections.heading: Why older Chicago buildings change the job
sections.body: Much of the north and northwest side predates 1940. Those buildings were wired for lighting and have had loads added ever since, so 100A services and crowded panels are common. Brick walls lengthen conduit routes. Two-flats raise the question of which meter the array serves, and converted condos need association approval for the shared roof.

sections.heading: How the City and ComEd steps fit together
sections.body: The City issues the permit and inspects the work. ComEd approves the interconnection and grants approval to operate. Both have their own timelines, and the system stays off until both are done. That is why we schedule around them rather than promise a date we can't hold.

sections.heading: Repairing arrays from closed installers
sections.body: Equipment warranties usually sit with the manufacturer, so they can outlive the installer. Diagnosis comes first: the symptom points to where to look, and the error code and monitoring history narrow it down. If a part is discontinued, the replacement can change the wiring, and we tell you that before quoting.

faqs.question: How long does a solar inverter last?
faqs.answer: Inverters usually need attention long before the panels do. The make, model and operating conditions decide the actual life, so we read the error history before recommending a replacement.

faqs.question: Can you replace an inverter on a system you did not install?
faqs.answer: Yes. Bring the inverter make and model, a photo of the error and the monitoring login if you have it.

faqs.question: Can I add a battery to my existing inverter?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. It depends on the inverter model. Hybrid inverters are built for it; others need an AC-coupled battery. We check before recommending equipment.

faqs.question: Why does my inverter keep shutting off?
faqs.answer: Common causes are grid voltage at the edge of its range, a loose connection or overheating. The error log usually tells us which.

faqs.question: Will my inverter work during a power outage?
faqs.answer: Not on its own. A grid-tied inverter shuts off when the grid goes down so it can't feed lines crews are working on. Backup needs a battery and a backup-capable setup.

faqs.question: My installer went out of business. Who handles the warranty?

serviceGuide.heading: Dimmers and LED lighting: the practical detail
serviceGuide.intro: Dimmers were designed for incandescent bulbs. LED lighting changed the rules, which is why so many dimmers flicker, buzz or stop at half brightness.

sections.heading: Why LEDs and old dimmers don't mix
sections.body: Older dimmers were designed for the steady load of incandescent bulbs. LED bulbs draw far less power and use electronics that react differently, which shows up as flicker, buzz or a limited dimming range.

sections.heading: Minimum load
sections.body: Many dimmers need a minimum total load to work smoothly. A few low-wattage LEDs may fall below it. The fix is a dimmer with a lower minimum, or adjusting its range.

sections.heading: Several dimmers in one box
sections.body: When dimmers share a box, their ratings usually drop because heat has less room to escape. We check the total load against the derated rating.

sections.heading: Smart dimmers in older homes
sections.body: Many smart dimmers need a neutral wire in the switch box. In older Chicago homes it is often missing. Some models work without one; otherwise new wiring is needed.

faqs.question: How long must emergency lights run on battery?
faqs.answer: The common standard is 90 minutes. [CONFIRM: the requirement the City applies to each building type]

faqs.question: How often should exit signs be tested?
faqs.answer: The common standard (NFPA 101) calls for a short functional test monthly and a full-duration test yearly. [CONFIRM: the schedule Chicago enforces]

faqs.question: Why does my emergency light fail the test?
faqs.answer: Usually a worn-out battery, a failed charger or a lost supply. Testing tells us which.

faqs.question: Can you replace just the battery?
faqs.answer: Yes, when the unit and charger are sound and the right battery is available.

faqs.question: Do new exit signs need a permit?

faqs.question: Can you give us a testing record?

serviceGuide.title: Exit Sign & Egress Lighting — Detail
serviceGuide.heading: Egress lighting requirements: the practical detail
serviceGuide.intro: Egress lighting is about the path out of a building: corridors, stairs and exits. When normal power fails, it has to light that path on its own.

sections.heading: What egress lighting is for
sections.body: When normal power fails, people still need to find the way out. Exit signs mark the route; emergency lights make it visible. Both have to work on their own power.

sections.heading: Battery duration and testing
sections.body: Battery-backed units are commonly required to run for 90 minutes. Batteries wear out, which is why regular testing matters more than the fixture itself.

sections.heading: Older Chicago buildings
sections.body: Walk-up and courtyard buildings often have long corridors and stairs fed by few circuits. Adding units sometimes means adding an unswitched supply, which is the part that takes time.

sections.heading: Inspection notices
sections.body: A notice lists specific items. Correcting exactly those, and recording the tests, is the fastest route to a passed re-inspection.
